analysis.one_liner: Funds heating aid for low-income households by ending a tax deduction for major oil companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added $2.53 billion in emergency funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), which helps low-income families pay heating and cooling bills. To pay for it, the bill would have taken away a tax deduction that major integrated oil companies (the large firms that produce, refine, and sell oil and gas) currently claim on income from domestic oil and gas production. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that qualify for LIHEAP would gain help paying home heating and cooling bills, and the state agencies that distribute the aid would get more money to hand out. The cost would fall entirely on major integrated oil companies, which would lose the domestic production deduction on income from oil and gas production, refining, and distribution.

how_it_helps.text: It appropriates an additional $2.53 billion for FY2008 LIHEAP payments to states, including $1.265 billion for regular allotments and $1.265 billion for emergency contingency funds, money that helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills.

It pays for that aid by denying major integrated oil companies the domestic production tax deduction for income from producing, refining, processing, transporting, or distributing oil and gas, effective for tax years after 2008.

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies, which would lose a recurring tax deduction on income from domestic oil and gas production and related activities.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the domestic production deduction raises oil companies' costs, which the industry argued could discourage domestic energy production and be passed to consumers through higher fuel prices.
The LIHEAP money was a one-time emergency appropriation for FY2008; it would not fix the underlying gap between the program's funding and low-income households' year-to-year energy needs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a straightforward trade: a permanent tax break for five of the largest and most profitable companies converted into heating aid for low-income households during a year of record energy prices. The main objection is that repealing the deduction could slightly reduce domestic drilling and refining activity, and some argue oil companies would pass costs to consumers at the pump. Against that, the targeted families facing utility shutoffs in winter were the clear focus of the bill, and the cost to the companies was a small share of their domestic income.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced any further before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 17, 2008, during a summer of record oil and gasoline prices.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, and no further action was taken.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without the committee or the Senate acting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies kept the domestic production tax deduction, and low-income households did not receive the additional heating assistance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies kept the deduction

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its funding and tax provisions.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action, never scheduling a markup or vote.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Major integrated oil companies and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed repealing oil and gas tax breaks during the 2008 energy price debates.

sides.party_line_note: Both named sponsors were Republicans, and no votes were ever taken, so no party breakdown of support or opposition exists in the record.

industries.industry: Major integrated oil and gas companies
industries.note: The bill would deny the section 199 domestic production tax deduction on income from producing, refining, transporting, and distributing oil and gas, a recurring tax benefit worth billions to the largest firms.
State LIHEAP agencies would receive $2.53 billion more to distribute as heating assistance, a direct gain for eligible low-income households and the agencies that serve them.
